lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: So you finally made it down to us, Polystratus. You lived what — nearly a hundred years, if I'm counting right?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Ninety-eight, Simylus.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: And how exactly did those last thirty go? You were around seventy when I died.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Superbly. I know that'll sound strange to you.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: It does, rather. Old, frail, no children — and you managed to enjoy yourself?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: In the early part of it, all that was still available to me — beautiful boys, the most delicate women, perfume, wine that smelled of flowers, a table that would have embarrassed anything in Sicily.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: This is news to me. I always knew you as a man who kept his hand firmly on his purse.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Ah, but the good things came to me from other people, my friend. Every morning, first thing, a very large number of callers at the door. And after that, gifts of every description, the finest things from every corner of the earth.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Did you become a tyrant after I died, Polystratus?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No. I had ten thousand admirers.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: [laughs] Admirers. You. At that age. With four teeth.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: The very finest men in the city, I assure you. Old as I was, bald as you see me, dribbling, runny-nosed — they competed to attend to me. And the man I so much as glanced at considered himself blessed.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: You didn't perhaps ferry some goddess across from Chios, the way Phaon did? She granted him youth and beauty and desirability all over again?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Nothing like that. I was exactly as you see me, and they adored me for it.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: You're speaking in riddles.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Surely it's perfectly obvious. There is a very powerful passion directed at old men who are rich and childless.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Now I understand the source of your beauty, you remarkable man. It came from the golden Aphrodite.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: And I got considerable use out of my admirers, Simylus — they practically prostrated themselves. I played hard to get. I shut the door on some of them occasionally. They raced each other to outdo one another in their attentions to me.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: And in the end — what did you decide to do with the estate?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: To each of them in turn I would announce, openly, that I was leaving him the inheritance. He would believe it and redouble his flattery. But I had a separate will — the real one — and when I was done I left them all to weep, once they'd been informed.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: And who did the real will name? Someone from the family, presumably?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Not at all. A recently purchased Phrygian slave boy. One of the pretty ones. About twenty.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Twenty. [pause] Yes, I think I understand what he was providing in return.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Even so, he deserved the inheritance far more than they did — barbarian, reprobate, and all, the same one the respectable gentlemen are already lining up to flatter. He inherited, and now he is counted among the nobility: clean-shaven, still mangling his Greek, but declared nobler than Codrus, handsomer than Nireus, cleverer than Odysseus.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: I don't particularly care. Let him command all of Greece if he likes. Just as long as those others don't get a penny.
